div.head: Ger 3
div.ab: [3] Gyf he wel aginnan wile, ne mæig he sleac beon ne to oferhydig; ac he mot ægðer witan ge læsse ge mare, ge betere ge mætre ðæs ðe to tune belimpð, ge on tune ge on dune, ge on wuda ge on wætere, ge on felda ge on falde, ge inne ge ute.

Gyf he wel aginnan wile ne mæig he sleac beon ne to ofer hydig ac he mot ægðer witan ge læsse ge mare ge betere ge mætre ðæs ðe to tune belimpð . ge on tune . ge on dune . ge on wuda . ge on wæ|tere. ge on felda. ge on falda . ge inne . ge ute.

Gyf he wel aginnan wile, ne mæig he sleac beon ne to oferhydig, ac he mot ægðer witan ge læsse ge mare, ge betere ge mætre ðæs ðe to tune belimpð, ge on tune ge on dune, ge on wuda ge on wætere, ge on felda ge on falde, ge inne ge ute.

Wenn er wohl beginnen will, darf er nicht schlaff noch zu stolz sein; sondern er muss kennen sowohl kleineres wie grösseres, so besseres wie geringeres dessen, was zum Landgute gehört, sowohl im Dorfbezirk wie auf dem Hügel, so im Walde wie im Wasser, so auf der Ackerflur wie in der Hürde, so drinnen wie draussen.

If he wishes to begin well [to work successfully], he must not be slack nor too proud [careless]; but he must know both the lesser and the greater, the better and the poorer of what belongs to the estate, both in the village [with the manor-house and arable, as opposed to the pasture outside] and on the down, in the wood and in the water, in the field and in the fold, indoors and out.

If he wants to perform well, he must not be slack nor over-cautious, but he must know both the lesser and the greater, both the better and the poorer of that which pertains to the estate, both in the farmyard and on the hills, both in the woodlands and on the waters, both in the fields and the folds, both indoors and outdoors.

If he desires to do well, he must be neither slack nor overcautious, but he must know both the lesser things and the greater, the better things and the worse, of all that belongs to the estate, both on the homestead and in the hills, both in the woods and in the waters, both in the fields and in the folds, both indoors and out.
div.note: B's ‘wile’ stands so. Liebermann notes that Cato (De re rustica V) demands of the bailiff: ‘opus rusticum omne curet, uti sciat facere, et id faciat saepe, dum ne lassus fiat’. ‘tune … dune’ is a rhyming pair, the others alliterate. K: ‘æðger’ corrected to ‘ægðer’.

See above 1³. On the following l. cf. Tusser (16th cent.) LIII, 8: in the toun as the field, where, however, toun already means ‘place of residence’ alone
samt Herrenhaus und Ackerflur, im Gegensatz zur Weide draussen
together with the manor house and the arable fields, in contrast to the pasture outside
